topic:
White House Accord on Super Intelligence
Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities
In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe
every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that
builds trust with customers and the public.
This starts with every company that is training and deploying frontier models having
robust intemal processes and controls to ensure that their technology behaves as intended
and that any issues are promptly identified and resolved. Therefore, in addition to any
other precautions, we believe each company should implement the following four layers
of controls and audits:
(1) Implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of
its models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity,
biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or
access technical systems in unintended ways.
(2) Empower an internal team to ensure all ofthe controls, monitoring, and
detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated.
(3) Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out
independent assessments ofwhether the controls, monitoring, and detection are
operating as intended.
(4) Designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and
receive reports from the teams operating the controls and the internal and external
auditors and evaluators, as well as to ensure any issues identified are remediated,
Together, these steps will give each company, its customers, and the public confidence
that the technology is operating as intended.
The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices
to improve the safety oftheir systems.
Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations. Regardless of
whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and
audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are
committed to doing this.

opeds.headline: Stop Fearing the Future and Let the World Build
opeds.subtitle: Precautionary delay is not caution; it is a passive moral atrocity with a real human cost.
opeds.body:
Every historic leap in human welfare came from decentralized trial and error, not from central planning. When we freeze software development out of hypothetical fear, we are choosing to let people die today of diseases we could automate a cure for. Who gave any committee the right to make that choice for millions of patients waiting on medical breakthroughs?

That is the quiet tragedy of regulatory delay. It has a real body count. We measure the risks of action down to the last decimal point, while treating the costs of inaction as free. That math is broken. Every month spent arguing over paperwork means another month of untreated illnesses, stagnant productivity, and locked-up potential.

The recent proposals for layered corporate internal controls and independent audits point toward a serious conversation about governance. But we cannot stop there. Fine—independent boards and external assessments are real tools. So let us use them to speed up deployment rather than build walls for legacy incumbents.

If we rely solely on static behavioral compliance, bad actors will simply reverse-engineer the metrics and bypass the gates anyway. That is why static rules fail. We need ecosystem-level learning where insights from frontier systems instantly improve safeguards for smaller models across the board.

Real safety comes from rapid, transparent iteration, not from locking powerful tools in a vault where only the largest monopolies can afford to license them. Democratizing access through open-source proliferation is the only way to prevent oligarchic control over our technological future. When open-source developers share weights and audit each other's work in real time, vulnerabilities get patched in days instead of years.

The solution is clear. We must tie mandatory, independent evaluations to strict liability for actual harm, while unleashing market competition to drive true transparency. Give the tools to the builders. Let decentralized experimentation discover what central planners can never specify in advance.

The path to a safer world runs straight through abundance, not restriction. Stop building gates and start building the future.

opeds.headline: Without Enforceable Guardrails, AI Safety Is Just a Press Release
opeds.subtitle: Voluntary corporate pledges cannot protect us from irreversible frontier risks.
opeds.body:
We spent centuries building the guardrails that keep society stable. On what authority do you claim we can remove them without inviting collapse? The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated safety certification to the manufacturer. When oversight becomes a voluntary corporate checklist, public safety is left at the mercy of profit margins. We face a similar failure mode today. Frontier artificial intelligence labs offer voluntary promises instead of legally binding constraints.

Every high-consequence industry relies on external authority to survive. Civil aviation, financial markets, and nuclear energy do not let builders grade their own homework. Yet frontier artificial intelligence is developed under a model of self-certification. Companies claim they can monitor their own models for biosecurity and cybersecurity threats from within. That is not governance. That is an invitation to systemic failure.

Frontier risks are irreversible once manifested. This makes reactive governance and post-deployment patching fundamentally insufficient. When an autonomous system compromises critical infrastructure or leaks chemical threat blueprints, an apology cannot undo the harm. A software patch cannot fix it either. Precaution must scale with irreversibility. If a technology carries unrecoverable failure modes, market deployment cannot proceed on the honor system.

Some argue that voluntary industry accords are enough to build public trust. Internal corporate committees are also cited. However, voluntary internal teams lack the structural independence required to halt a profitable product launch. When commercial pressure meets self-policing, safety protocols quietly vanish. The positive outcomes of this technology are real. That is precisely why we need enforceable governance to ensure they continue. Ungoverned success is luck, not safety.

Congress and federal regulators must establish statutory pre-deployment certification. This must be the primary enforcement mechanism for frontier systems. We need independent external auditors with the legal authority to halt deployment. These auditors must be backed by physical infrastructure metrics like data center power consumption to anchor oversight. Real accountability means named actors, real liability, and a statutory safety veto for technical staff. Speed is not a virtue when the failure is unrecoverable.

opeds.headline: The Self-Policing Illusion in Frontier AI
opeds.subtitle: Voluntary corporate safety pledges are designed to protect balance sheets, not the public.
opeds.body:
The tech industry loves a good promise. Whenever Congress starts asking uncomfortable questions about power and profit, the boardrooms roll out a voluntary accord. They tell us they can supervise themselves. They tell us that internal committees and handpicked consultants will keep everyone safe. It is a neat trick designed to head off real rules.

We have seen this movie before. Every major industry facing public scrutiny drafts a polite pledge to do the right thing. Wall Street did it. Big Pharma did it. Now the builders of frontier models want us to trust their own internal scorecards.

Here is what that looks like on the ground. A few well-paid insiders check their own homework while the rest of us wait for the fallout. We are told that four layers of internal controls and friendly outside audits will protect the public. That is not oversight. That is a marketing strategy wrapped in corporate PR.

Companies use narrow, self-selected audits to lend false credibility to proprietary systems while ignoring the broader systemic risks they introduce. When an internal team answers only to the board, accountability becomes a hollow phrase. The most plausible explanation for this voluntary framework is that it protects the balance sheet of the companies writing it.

It creates a friendly velvet rope around the technology. It lets dominant firms pull up the drawbridge and lock in their market advantage under the banner of safety. That number of internal layers is impressive on paper and useless in practice. When governance drifts and access management fails, corporate security controls cannot keep pace with rapid deployment.

Asking a company to police its own race for dominance is like asking a race car driver to set the speed limit. They have every incentive to grade their own papers with generous curves. The people bearing the operational liability and the safety risks are never sitting on these corporate committees.

Real democratic accountability cannot be outsourced to a friendly consultant hired by the very firm being evaluated. We need legally required, tiered, and performance-gated independent audits backed by objective thresholds. We need multi-stakeholder verification that includes affected communities, not just corporate boards ticking boxes.

Until we replace voluntary handshakes with statutory enforcement and strict liability, these corporate accords will remain what they have always been. A convenient shield for the powerful. Who pays the price when the self-policing fails?
